953.title: The hiding place
953.hook: the ten Boom family, Dutch watchmakers, hide Jews in a secret room; Corrie later forgives a guard
953.howItsDone: The ten Boom house in Haarlem is now a museum where visitors can see the hiding place, and Corrie ten Boom's story of forgiving a guard is often told in churches, especially among evangelical Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maximilian Kolbe stepped out of line. Your line was let me go instead. Whose small turn did you take? Day nine hundred fifty-three.

Clocks tick along the walls of a narrow house in Haarlem, in the Netherlands. Downstairs is the family watch shop. Upstairs, at the top of a steep staircase, is a small bedroom, and at the back of that bedroom is a wall that isn't quite where it should be. Behind it there's a space barely deep enough for people to stand in a row, with a little vent for air. When the buzzer sounds, the people living in the house have a short time to climb in, close the panel, and be silent. Today, the hiding place.

The ten Booms were Dutch Reformed Christians, an old watchmaker, Casper, and his grown daughters Betsie and Corrie, who opened their home to Jews and to members of the resistance when the Nazis occupied their country. The secret room was built behind a false wall in Corrie's bedroom. Then someone betrayed them. Police raided the house and arrested the family. They never found the room, and the people hiding inside it got out alive. The ten Booms were not so fortunate. Casper died after a short time in prison. Corrie and Betsie were sent to the women's camp at Ravensbrück, and Betsie died there. Corrie was released, and after the war she traveled and told the story, and later she told it in a book, The Hiding Place. The title echoes a psalm. In the King James Bible: "Thou art my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word." A family hid people, and trusted that they themselves were hidden in God. Then comes the harder part. After the war, after speaking at a church in Germany about forgiveness, Corrie saw a man coming toward her with his hand out. She recognized him as a guard from Ravensbrück. By her own telling, she couldn't lift her hand. She felt nothing warm toward him at all. She prayed for help, and she took his hand, and only then, she said, did the feeling come. She didn't describe forgiveness as forgetting, or as saying it didn't matter. She described it as an act she chose before she could feel it, with help from beyond herself. Her story is often told in churches, and some readers also say gently that no one should be rushed into that handshake.

Here's the practice: look at one thing that seemed impossible to forgive. Go gently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something someone did that you've never let go of. Not the worst thing in your life, unless you're ready. Something you can look at. Notice how your hand feels as you think of it. Clenched, maybe. You don't have to forgive it today. Just notice whether you'd like to, someday. Corrie's way was to ask for help before the feeling came. If you pray, you can ask for that help. If you don't, just open your hand on your knee, and see what it's like to hold it open. The bell holds the time.
The hiding place. A secret room in a watchmaker's house where the ten Booms hid Jews, and a line from the psalms about being hidden in God.
Your line: the hiding place. Today, be a safe place for one person, someone who needs a door that opens, or a hand that isn't closed. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: Mother Maria Skobtsova
954.hook: an Orthodox nun in Paris hides Jews and dies in Ravensbrück
954.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians remember Saint Maria of Paris together with Father Dimitri Klepinin, her son Yuri and their companions, and her writings on love of neighbor are read in parishes and study groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hiding place behind a false wall in Haarlem, and a hand Corrie couldn't lift. Who were you a safe place for? Day nine hundred fifty-four.

A nun in a black habit is haggling at the market in Paris at dawn, buying the cheap end of the vegetables, then hauling the sacks back through the streets herself. She has been a poet, a revolutionary, a mayor in her old Russian town, a wife twice, a mother. Her house on the rue de Lourmel is full of people nobody else wants: the homeless, the drunk, the broke, the mentally ill. Some of the church people are scandalized. A nun should be in a monastery, praying. She thinks she is praying. Today, Mother Maria.

She was born Elizaveta in the Russian Empire and left after the revolution, like other Russians who ended up as refugees in Paris. After the death of one of her children, her life turned. She became an Orthodox nun, Mother Maria, but with her bishop's blessing she lived in the city, not behind walls. Her monastery, she liked to say, was the whole world. Her idea was simple and hard. Every person is an image of God, an icon. Orthodox Christians honor icons in church: they kiss them, bow to them, light candles before them. So, she said, why not bow to the living icon in front of you, the hungry man at the door? The carry today, the sacrament of the brother, is a phrase people link with her. The altar is holy, and so is your brother. The First Letter of John puts it sharply. In the King James Bible: "he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" Then the Nazis took Paris. Jews were ordered to wear a yellow star, and her house became a hiding place. With a priest of the house, Father Dimitri Klepinin, she gave Jews baptismal papers that might protect them, and she helped hide people and get them out. The Gestapo arrested them both, and her son Yuri. All three died in the camps. Mother Maria was sent to Ravensbrück, the same camp where Betsie ten Boom died. Some accounts say she took another woman's place in the line for the gas chamber. The sources are honest that nobody knows for sure. Orthodox Christians now honor her as a saint, with Father Dimitri and Yuri.
screen: `A NUN WHOSE MONASTERY WAS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for someone in danger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is at risk right now. Not in a history book. In your life or your news. Someone sick, someone being bullied, someone afraid of losing a home or a job, someone far away in a war. Mother Maria looked at the person at the door the way people look at an icon. Try it for a moment. See the face. Let it be holy. Then ask what one small thing would make that person a little safer. If you pray, you can say the line from First John quietly. The bell holds the time.
Mother Maria Skobtsova. A Russian Orthodox nun in Paris who ran a house for the poor, helped Jews hide, and died in Ravensbrück.
Your line: the sacrament of the brother. Today, treat one person you'd usually walk past as if they were holy: eye contact, a name, a real answer. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

955.title: Edith Stein
955.hook: a Jewish-born philosopher who became a Carmelite nun and was killed at Auschwitz
955.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross each August, and Carmelites honor her as one of their own; her philosophical writings are studied in universities, and some Catholic and Jewish groups remember her together in Holocaust remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mother Maria, who saw every person as an icon. Your line was the sacrament of the brother. Who did you stop and see? Day nine hundred fifty-five.

A guest in a friend's house can't sleep, so she pulls a book off the shelf. It's the life of Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish nun, written in her own words. The guest is a philosopher, sharp, trained to take ideas apart, and for years she has had no religious faith at all. She reads through the night. When she closes the book, tradition says, she tells herself: this is the truth. Her name is Edith Stein. She was born into a Jewish family, and the road that night opens will end in a place no one would choose. Today, Edith Stein.

Edith Stein grew up in an observant Jewish home with a mother she loved deeply. As a young woman she left faith behind and went into philosophy, studying under Edmund Husserl, a founder of phenomenology, the careful study of experience as it's lived. She wrote on empathy: how we can know what another person goes through. After that night with Teresa, she was baptized a Catholic, which grieved her mother. Years later she entered a Carmelite convent, the order Teresa had reformed, and took a new name, Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. She never stopped seeing herself as a daughter of the Jewish people. As Nazi persecution grew, her order moved her to a convent in the Netherlands for safety. Then the Dutch Catholic bishops publicly protested the deportation of Jews. The occupiers struck back by arresting Catholics of Jewish birth. Edith was taken with her sister Rosa, who had also become Catholic. By the account of witnesses, Edith took Rosa's hand and said, come, we are going for our people. She was murdered at Auschwitz. In a letter, she had compared herself to Queen Esther, who stood before the king to plead for her people. In the King James Bible, Esther says: "let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request." The Catholic Church has named her a saint and a martyr. Some Jewish voices have asked, fairly, that this not blur a plain fact: the Nazis killed her because she was born a Jew. Both things are part of her story. Honoring her means holding all of it.
screen: `COME, WE ARE GOING FOR OUR PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone's whole story. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person you tend to describe with one label. The convert. The one who left. The religious one. The difficult one. Edith Stein is easy to shrink to one line too. Now let the rest of their story come in. Where they started. What they lost. What they kept. Who they still belong to. Let the label get smaller and the person get bigger. If you pray, you can hold that whole person before God. If you don't, just hold them, whole, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Edith Stein. A philosopher born into a Jewish family, who became a Carmelite nun and was murdered at Auschwitz.
Your line: for my people. Today, ask one person a question about where they come from, and listen to the answer all the way to the end. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Takashi Nagai
956.hook: a Catholic doctor in Nagasaki who kept treating the wounded after the bomb killed his wife
956.howItsDone: In Nagasaki, Nagai's hut is preserved beside a memorial museum, and Catholics in the Urakami community remember the bombing each August with Mass and prayer for peace at the rebuilt cathedral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edith Stein, and her whole story. Your line was for my people. Whose story did you listen to, all the way to the end? Day nine hundred fifty-six.

In the ashes of a kitchen, a man kneels and picks up a few blackened bones, and beside them, a melted chain of rosary beads. He knows whose they are. He is a doctor, a radiologist, and a few days earlier he was at work in his hospital in Nagasaki when the atomic bomb fell. Bleeding from his own wounds, he spent those days treating other people. Only then did he come home to look for his wife, Midori. He carries what he found back in a bucket. Today, Takashi Nagai, and the bell that rang again.

Nagai grew up outside the church and came to Catholic faith as a young man, in Nagasaki's Urakami district, where Christian families had kept their faith in secret through long years of persecution. His wife Midori came from one of those families. By the time the bomb fell, he was already ill. Years of work with X-rays, without much protection, had given him leukemia. The bomb made everything worse. He set up first aid in the ruins, with the staff who were still alive, and worked until he collapsed. His children survived because they had been sent to the countryside. Afterward he lived with them in a tiny hut near the ruins of the cathedral. He named it for a line of Jesus. In the King James Bible: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." From his bed, as his illness grew, he wrote books, including one called The Bells of Nagasaki. The title comes from the cathedral. Its bells had been buried in the rubble, and when the people dug one out, it rang again, and to him it sounded like a promise that the city would live. Nagai also spoke of the bombing in religious terms, as a sacrifice, and other survivors and writers have strongly disagreed with that. It's fair to say his words comforted some and troubled others. What's harder to argue with is what he did with his hands. He grieved and he worked, both at once. Jesus said, in Matthew: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Nagai didn't wait to be comforted before he started caring for others.
screen: `A HUT NAMED FOR LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.`
`THE BELL DUG OUT OF THE RUBBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care while grieving. Settle, and breathe. If you're carrying a loss right now, a person, a place, a plan, let yourself name it. Don't hurry it away. Then notice who else is near you who might need something. A child. A friend. A coworker who looks tired. Nagai didn't wait until his grief was finished. Ask what one small act of care you could do today, not instead of grieving but alongside it. If you're not grieving now, bring to mind someone who is, and what might help them. If you pray, you can say the line from Matthew: blessed are they that mourn. The bell holds the time.
Takashi Nagai. A Catholic doctor in Nagasaki who lost his wife to the atomic bomb, kept treating the wounded, and wrote The Bells of Nagasaki.
Your line: the bells of nagasaki. Today, if you hear a bell, a chime or a phone alert, let it remind you of one person to care for, even on a heavy day. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Mere Christianity on the radio
957.hook: during the war, C. S. Lewis gave BBC talks explaining the faith plainly
957.howItsDone: Some Christians explain their faith in ordinary conversation rather than formal argument, and some church study groups and curious readers still read Lewis's talks, gathered as the book Mere Christianity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takashi Nagai, the doctor in Nagasaki who kept caring for the wounded while he grieved his wife. Your line was the bells of Nagasaki. What rang out of a hard place for you? Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

A radio sits on a shelf in a front room in wartime Britain. The blackout curtains are drawn. It is evening, and a different voice comes on. Not a bishop. Not a preacher with a pulpit voice. A teacher from Oxford, talking about right and wrong, and why people keep arguing about fairness as if they all expected there to be such a thing. He talks the way you'd talk to a friend across the table. He uses examples from queues and quarrels and schoolyards. The BBC had asked him to explain the Christian faith, out loud, to a country at war. His name was C. S. Lewis. Today, the talks that later became a book.

Lewis was a layman. He taught literature, he belonged to the Church of England, and he was clear that he spoke for no church officially. That mattered to him. He didn't want to use the microphone to argue for his own church against the others. He wanted to lay out the ground that Christians of different churches hold in common, and leave the questions that divide them to each church to teach. He called that shared ground mere Christianity. Mere here doesn't mean small or slight. Some readers hear an older sense of the word in it: plain, just this, with nothing added. In the preface to the book, he gives a picture for it. Mere Christianity, he says, is like a hall in a large house, with doors opening off it into rooms. The hall is a place to wait, to find your way, but not a place to live. The rooms are where the fires and the chairs and the meals are, and those rooms are the churches. He hoped people would find their room. And he asked those in one room to be kind to those who had chosen another door. Why plain words? There's an old instruction in the first letter of Peter, in the King James Bible: "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." A reason, not a shout. An answer, given with meekness. Lewis tried to do that for listeners at home in wartime, who had no time for long words. Plain is not the same as simple-minded. It is harder. You have to know a thing well before you can say it short.
screen: `A REASON FOR THE HOPE, WITH MEEKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one belief plainly. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing Christians believe, or one thing you believe yourself. Grace. Forgiveness. Resurrection. That people matter. Now try to say it in two short sentences, the way you'd say it to a curious kid on a walk. No jargon. No winning. If a word feels too big, swap it for a smaller one. Then let the sentences rest, and breathe with them. If you pray, you can ask for meekness when you speak about what you hope. The bell holds the time.
Mere Christianity on the radio. The wartime BBC talks in which C. S. Lewis explained the faith Christians share, in plain words, later gathered into a book.
screen: `MERE CHRISTIANITY ON THE RADIO — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: plain words in wartime. Today, when something hard needs saying, say it short, say it plain, and say it kindly. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: The World Council of Churches (1948)
958.hook: churches from many traditions meet to pray and work together
958.howItsDone: Member churches send delegates to the council's assemblies and committees, and in some towns local churches of different traditions keep a week of prayer for Christian unity together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mere Christianity on the radio, and a picture of a hall with doors into many rooms. Your line was plain words in wartime. What did you manage to say plainly? Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

"That they all may be one." In John's Gospel, Jesus prays those words for his followers on the night before he dies. Christians have read them aloud in churches that, for long stretches, would not share a table, a pulpit or a cup. Now come forward to the years just after the Second World War. Much of Europe is in ruins. Churches that had prayed on opposite sides of the war send people to Amsterdam: Protestants and Anglicans, Orthodox churches of the East, delegates from Asia, Africa and the Americas. They pray together. They argue. And they decide to form a council and keep meeting. Today, a table with many churches at it.

The first thing to know is what the World Council of Churches is not. It isn't a super-church. Nobody leaves their own church to join it, and it doesn't tell its members what to believe. It describes itself as a fellowship of churches that confess Jesus Christ as God and Savior, according to the scriptures, and try together to live out that calling. Each church keeps its own worship, its own leaders, its own teaching. They meet as guests at one table. The message from that first gathering in Amsterdam is remembered for a simple resolve: the churches meant to stay together. Not merge. Stay. The second thing is who sits at the table. Protestant and Anglican churches, and Orthodox churches of the East, are among its members. The Catholic Church is not a member, but it has worked alongside the council, and each year the materials for a week of prayer for Christian unity are prepared by both together. Some churches choose to stay outside altogether, for reasons they take seriously: a worry that unity could blur what they believe, or a different understanding of what the church is. Those are honest convictions, not failures of goodwill. The third thing is what they actually do. They pray. They study the hard questions, like baptism and communion, side by side, and write down where they agree and where they don't. And they work: refugees, relief after disasters, peace talks, hunger. Jesus's prayer in John is a prayer, not a plan. The council is one attempt to take it seriously, with all the slowness that real agreement takes.

Here's the practice: pray with another church, or hold one in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of a church that isn't yours, or isn't the one you grew up near. The Orthodox parish with the onion domes. The storefront church with the hand-painted sign. The cathedral downtown. Picture the people who will gather there this week. Their kitchen, their choir, their worries. If you pray, you can borrow Jesus's own words for them and for you: that they all may be one. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, by name if you know it. The bell holds the time.
The World Council of Churches. A fellowship of churches from many traditions that meet to pray, study and work together, each keeping its own life.
screen: `THE WORLD COUNCIL OF CHURCHES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: together. Today, do one ordinary thing alongside someone who sees the world differently from you: share a meal, finish a task, take a walk. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Billy Graham
959.hook: an American evangelist preached to huge crowds worldwide and refused to hold segregated rallies
959.howItsDone: At evangelical revival meetings, the preacher often closes with an invitation to come forward, and counselors from local churches talk and pray with those who do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the World Council of Churches, many traditions at one table. Your line was together. Who did you do something ordinary alongside? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

The sermon is over. In a stadium full of people, a choir begins to sing, slowly, an old hymn: "Just as I am, without one plea." And people start to stand up. One here, a couple there, a teenager, a man in a work jacket. They make their way down the steps and across the grass toward the front, where the preacher waits. He has invited them to come, and he has told them their friends will wait for them. The preacher is Billy Graham, an evangelist from North Carolina, and this scene played out in city after city, across many countries. But part of his story isn't about people walking forward. It's about ropes.

Graham was a Baptist preacher, and his message was an invitation. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Graham preached that invitation in plain words, then asked people to answer it by coming forward. The hymn he used for that moment, written by Charlotte Elliott, says why you don't have to clean yourself up first. Just as I am. Without one plea. You come as you are, and the hymn leaves the rest to God. Now the ropes. In the American South of his early years, meetings could be divided by race, with ropes marking off where Black listeners could sit. Accounts of his life say that at one crusade in Tennessee, Graham took the ropes down himself. After that he refused to hold segregated meetings, and he invited Martin Luther King Jr. to pray at one of his crusades. Some civil rights leaders wished he had gone further, and said so. Both things are part of the record. Christians understand coming to faith in different ways. Evangelicals like Graham stress a personal decision to follow Christ, a moment you can point to. Other churches stress baptism, and a life of growing in faith, sometimes with no single moment to name. Graham's crusades worked with local churches and sent people back to them. In the hymn, just as I am is about how a person comes to God. Graham's ropes made it about who gets a seat, too.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite someone to something good. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who might like to be asked. A neighbor who's new. A friend who's been quiet lately. A cousin you never call. Now think of something good you could invite them to: a meal, a walk, a game, a concert, a service at your church if that's your world. When Philip in John's Gospel wanted to bring a friend to Jesus, he didn't argue. He said, come and see. Hold that person in mind, as they are. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Billy Graham. An American evangelist who invited crowds to come to Christ just as they were, and refused to hold segregated meetings.
